elements.quote: Since January 2021, the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), in collaboration with the National Immunisation Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) network coordinated by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) is performing a living systematic review on the efficacy, effectiveness and safety of coronavirus disease (COVID-19) vaccines authorised in the European Union (EU) (PROSPERO registration: CRD42020208935) [2].
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly describes the work as a 'living systematic review'.

elements.quote: We summarised the evidence on COVID19 vaccine effectiveness (VE) identified in 17 studies that investigated VE against different endpoints. ... Here we present results on the effectiveness and the duration of protection provided by the EU-licensed COVID-19 vaccines in respect to the Delta variant.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main objective: summarising evidence on vaccine effectiveness and duration of protection against the Delta variant.

elements.quote: had a comparison group that investigated vaccine effectiveness (VE) against SARS-CoV-2 infection of any severity after vaccination with a COVID-19 vaccine (see Supplement Part S2 for complete population intervention comparison outcomes (PICO) question) approved by the European Medicines Agency. We did not apply any restrictions on publication language and status.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies some inclusion features (studies with a comparison group; no language/status restrictions) and refers to a PICO in the supplement, but it does not provide full, explicit main inclusion and exclusion criteria in the abstract itself.

elements.quote: We searched the internal COVID-19 literature database constructed by the RKI library and hand-searched relevant websites (see [2] and Supplement Part S3 for description of the database and the search strategy). ... In total, 7,117 entries were identified and screened until 25 August 2021, the date of last search.
elements.reason: The abstract/related methods text identifies the information sources (internal RKI COVID-19 database and hand-searching relevant websites) and specifies the date of last search (25 August 2021).

elements.quote: The risk of bias in non-randomized studies - of interventions (ROBINS-I) was used to assess risk of bias [3].
elements.reason: The abstract/methods text states the tool used to assess risk of bias (ROBINS-I).

elements.quote: We performed meta-analyses, using a random-effects model to account for heterogeneity between studies. The I 2 was used to quantify the extent of heterogeneity. Formal testing for publication bias was done for datasets with 10 or more estimates by inspection of funnel plots, followed by Begg's test and Egger's test (Supplement Part S4).
elements.reason: The abstract describes the synthesis methods (random-effects meta-analysis, use of I2 for heterogeneity, and publication bias assessment).

elements.quote: We summarised the evidence on COVID19 vaccine effectiveness (VE) identified in 17 studies that investigated VE against different endpoints.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (17) and the types of endpoints assessed, but it does not report the total number of participants or provide a fuller summary of study characteristics (e.g., study designs and settings) in the abstract.

elements.quote: Pooled VE was 63.1% (95% confidence interval (CI): 40.9-76.9) against asymptomatic infection, 75.7% (95% CI: 69.3-80.8) against symptomatic infection and 90.9% (95% CI: 84.5-94.7) against hospitalisation.
elements.reason: The abstract presents results for the main outcomes with pooled estimates and confidence intervals (and overall number of studies earlier).

elements.quote: Pooled VE was 63.1% (95% confidence interval (CI): 40.9-76.9) against asymptomatic infection, 75.7% (95% CI: 69.3-80.8) against symptomatic infection and 90.9% (95% CI: 84.5-94.7) against hospitalisation.
elements.reason: A meta-analysis was conducted and the abstract reports the summary estimates with 95% confidence intervals for main outcomes.

elements.quote: Compared with the Alpha variant, VE against mild outcomes was reduced by 10-20%, but fully maintained against severe COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract compares groups (Delta vs Alpha), indicates the direction of effect (reduced VE for mild outcomes with Delta) and which outcome is favored (Alpha for mild outcomes; no reduction for severe outcomes).

The abstract does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (risk of bias, inconsistency, or imprecision). Limitations appear in the Discussion section but are not presented in the abstract text provided.

elements.quote: Compared with the Alpha variant, VE against mild outcomes was reduced by 10-20%, but fully maintained against severe COVID-19.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of results and their implications regarding maintained effectiveness against severe disease despite reduced protection for milder outcomes.
No statement of the primary source of funding for the review is present in the abstract or provided evidence.

elements.quote: PROSPERO registration: CRD42020208935
elements.reason: The abstract provides the name of the register (PROSPERO) and the registration number.

elements.quote: The Delta variant (Phylogenetic Assignment of Named Global Outbreak (Pango) lineage designation B.1.617.2) of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) was first reported in October 2020 and has spread to more than 180 countries globally [1]. Concerns were raised about how well the currently available vaccines protect against this variant.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state (Delta variant emergence and global spread) and identifies an important uncertainty (concern about vaccine protection against Delta).

elements.quote: Since January 2021, the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), in collaboration with the National Immunisation Technical Advisory Groups (NITAGs) network coordinated by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) is performing a living systematic review on the efficacy, effectiveness and safety of coronavirus disease (COVID-19) vaccines authorised in the European Union (EU) (PROSPERO registration: CRD42020208935) [2]. Here we present results on the effectiveness and the duration of protection provided by the EU-licensed COVID-19 vaccines in respect to the Delta variant.
elements.reason: The manuscript explains the importance and need for the review (a living systematic review to summarise evidence on vaccine effectiveness against Delta) and states the review's purpose and registration.

elements.quote: As already discussed in the first interim analysis [2] and given the highly dynamic publishing landscape in this field, we cannot exclude the possibility that additional published studies were not captured by our search strategy.

elements.quote: These second interim results of our living systematic review show that COVID-19 vaccines approved in the EU have a moderate to high effectiveness against mild to moderate forms of SARS-CoV-2 infections caused by the Delta variant, while VE against severe disease and hospitalisation was high to very high. Statistical heterogeneity was low in meta-analysis of the severe outcomes, further supporting a well-maintained effectiveness against these endpoints under Delta variant dominance. In one study where VE was investigated in more than one age group, higher estimates in younger groups were seen. Of note, no VE estimate against Delta had been reported until data cut (25 August) for the Janssen vaccine. As already discussed in the first interim analysis [2] and given the highly dynamic publishing landscape in this field, we cannot exclude the possibility that additional published studies were not captured by our search strategy. Further limitations stem from the fact that genomic sequencing was used to determine VE against Delta in only a minority of studies, while in the majority of studies VE was estimated during time periods of dominant Delta circulation without sequencing. Moreover, based on the current evidence, it is challenging to segregate two factors contributing to the difference between the VE estimates against Alpha and Delta variants: waning immunity and actual VE against Delta. Furthermore, a number of studies did not report separate estimates per vaccine.
elements.reason: The discussion places the study findings (vaccine effectiveness against Delta for different severity levels) alongside other evidence: it references the first interim analysis, compares VE against Alpha vs Delta, notes age-group differences, discusses heterogeneity and methodological limitations (sequencing, potential missing studies), thereby interpreting results in the context of other relevant evidence.
